similar_scenes.name: DAF y el electropunk alemán
similar_scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
similar_scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
similar_scenes.desc: Estudiantes de arte de la pequeña escena de Düsseldorf, rebeldes contra «el imperialismo pop norteamericano»: en Mute, Die Kleinen und die Bösen es electropunk caótico; reducidos al dúo de Gabi Delgado y Robert Görl, en Virgin despojan su música hasta un «brutalismo eurodisco» y son estrellas en Alemania con Alles ist gut y «Der Mussolini». Primitivismo techno, culto al cuerpo, provocación con tabúes nazis y sexuales a lo Genet y Bataille: los verdaderos new romantics, inventores de la electronic body music e influencia en el house de Chicago y el techno de Detroit. Alrededor, Einstürzende Neubauten y Liaisons Dangereuses.

similar_scenes.name: Electronic Body Music
similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: Bélgica acuña una de las corrientes de baile industrial más exitosas, la «electronic body music», derivada del último Cabaret Voltaire con influencia disco y de ciencia ficción: Geography de Front 242 es el disco hito; después Klinik, Neon Judgement, Vomito Negro. En Vancouver, Skinny Puppy y Front Line Assembly, profetas de la generación cyberpunk. Los cimientos de la música de baile alternativa de los noventa.

similar_scenes.name: Electro: «Planet Rock» y el funk electrónico
similar_scenes.book: Techno Rebels: The Renegades of Electronic Funk
similar_scenes.author: Dan Sicko
similar_scenes.desc: La influencia directa de Kraftwerk sobre Afrika Bambaataa & the Soulsonic Force y el productor Arthur Baker dio «Planet Rock» (1982), que estalló en las pistas, definió el género electro (de «electronic funk») y cambió para siempre la manera de producir hip hop. Junto a Run-DMC y los Beastie Boys forma la combinación de rock y hip hop que luego la «electronica» explotaría.

similar_scenes.name: Industrial, EBM y The Final Cut
similar_scenes.book: Techno Rebels: The Renegades of Electronic Funk
similar_scenes.author: Dan Sicko
similar_scenes.desc: En 1989-1990 quien no escuchaba techno escuchaba industrial: Nitzer Ebb, Skinny Puppy, Front Line Assembly y los belgas Front 242 (Front by Front, 1988), con Chicago como centro americano (Ministry, Die Warzau, My Life with the Thrill Kill Kult, Wax Trax). Detroit tuvo su escena: Code Industry, el único grupo industrial enteramente afroamericano, y The Final Cut, de Jeff Mills y Tony Srock, banda de apoyo del grupo house True Faith (con Bridgett Grace) en Paragon, cuyo productor Jerry Capaldi acabó enfrentado a sus artistas y sembró desconfianza entre techno negro y blanco. Deep into the Cut (1990, Big Sex/Interfisch) cruzó EBM y techno; la última cita de Mills con ellos fue en el festival Atonal de Berlín. Srock los llevó hacia el rock (Consumed, Nettwerk, 1991).

similar_scenes.name: El festival de Detroit: DEMF y Movement
similar_scenes.book: Techno Rebels: The Renegades of Electronic Funk
similar_scenes.author: Dan Sicko
similar_scenes.desc: En mayo de 2000 Pop Culture Media y Carol Marvin, organizadora de los festivales de jazz, montaron el primer Detroit Electronic Music Festival, gratis, en Hart Plaza, con Carl Craig como director artístico. Al caer el sol del primer sábado, con el set de Stacey Pullen, la plaza estaba llena: la ciudad se reencontraba con su niño prodigio, Detroit por fin «entendía» el techno. (Se habló de un millón y medio de asistentes, cifra imposible.) En 2001 Marvin despidió a Craig justo antes del festival; él perdió la demanda pero ganó el voto popular («DEMF = Carl Craig»). Sobrevivió a tres cambios de dirección: Saunderson lo llevó en 2005 (Fuse-In) y dimitió, y en 2006 la ciudad se lo dio a Paxahau, que comprobó que el aforo de Hart Plaza era de 45.000 personas, cuidó el sonido y lo convirtió, con entrada de pago, en Movement, algo con lo que Detroit puede contar cada año. El techno ha perdido su misterio, pero la credibilidad de Detroit ya desborda sus calles.

podcast.title: Early Research Lab (1951)
podcast.body: A dedicated electronic lab was established in Cologne, West Germany, in 1951, indicating early institutional interest and development in electronic sound. "A special electronic lab was created in Cologne, West Germany in 1951."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD

podcast.title: Fusion with Psychedelia (1968)
podcast.body: By 1968, some enlightened young German musicians, grappling with their national identity, began to fuse these experimental electronic traditions with the psychedelic music prevalent at the time. Their objective was to forge a novel form of music that was independent of American or UK influences. "By 1968, some young enlightened musicians, those who were lost when it came to their identity as Germans, were involved in fusing these experimental electronic traditions with the psychedelic stuff of the day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 6

podcast.title: A Clockwork Orange Soundtrack (1972) as Landmark
podcast.body: The soundtrack for Stanley Kubrick's *A Clockwork Orange*, composed by Wendy Carlos (then Walter Carlos) using modular synthesizers, became a landmark in the development of electronic music for the masses. Its completely electronic and unheard sounds inspired rock musicians seeking new and different artistic directions. "It became a landmark in the development of electronic music for the masses."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Key Alt-Rock Movie Soundtracks

podcast.title: Pioneering Pilot (1981)
podcast.body: Gary Numan, recognized as an electronic music icon, demonstrated his versatility by becoming a highly accomplished pilot. In 1981, he completed a round-the-world flight in his private aircraft, a feat that highlighted his personal passions outside of his musical contributions. "Gary Newman, the new wave star, turned electronic icon to guys like Back in Dave Grohl, became very accomplished as a pilot, even working as a stunt pilot in air shows."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Airplanes!

podcast.title: Preference for "The World Is Not Enough" Theme (1999)
podcast.body: For the 1999 Bond film "The World Is Not Enough," producers sought an electronic sound for the theme song, reflecting modern music trends at the time. Despite this preference, they still insisted on a "big orchestral arrangement" to maintain the traditional Bond musical identity. "The producers wanted sort of an electronic sound. Again that's where modern music was in 1999."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Bond...James Bond...Music

podcast.title: Second Wave of Modern Electronic Music (2007)
podcast.body: The year 2007 marked a "second wave of modern electronic music," characterized by a resurgence of Daft Punk's influence, leading subsequent groups back towards a more minimalist, simpler, and purer path.

srcs.episode: Daft Punk: Como el Homework revolucionó la electrónica

podcast.title: John Frusciante's Post-RHCP Exploration (2009-2019)
podcast.body: After his second departure from the Red Hot Chili Peppers, John Frusciante's solo albums became very electronic, as he expressed a desire to try something he knew nothing about and had lost interest in traditional rock band songwriting. "He said he'd lost interest in traditional rock band songwriting and wanted to try something he knew nothing about."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Long Strange Trip of John Frusciante Part 2

podcast.title: 1990s Dominant Aesthetic
podcast.body: During the 1990s, the dominant electronic music scene followed a clear path, characterized by clean production, digital sound, and rhythm taking precedence over other elements. This musical approach reflected a societal obsession with constantly anticipating the future. "Durante los años 90 la música electrónica que dominaba la escena ha seguido un camino muy claro. La producción era limpia, el sonido digital, y la rímpica destacaba por encima de todos los elementos."

srcs.episode: El Género Musical Más Escalofriante de Internet. Hauntología

podcast.title: 80s Evolution and Limitations
podcast.body: During the 1980s, electronic pop and new wave music were characterized by their imaginative and fun qualities. However, they were generally considered to lack musical sophistication and complexity, often prioritizing the "idea" or concept over technical quality. "era muy imaginativa y era muy divertida pero musicalmente no era lo más sofisticado ni lo más complejo que había."

srcs.episode: Massive Attack - Blue Lines. Un antes y un después en la música.

podcast.title: 90s UK Context
podcast.body: Electronic music in the UK during the 1990s underwent a significant reinterpretation, largely spearheaded by The Chemical Brothers. This period was marked by the fusion of incoming Detroit Techno and Chicago House influences with existing local Manchester music at venues like The Hacienda, blending electronic and rock sounds. "una pizza clave dentro de la electrónica de los 90 en el reino unido y fueron el inicio de una reinterpretación electrónica muy interesante."

srcs.episode: The Chemical Brothers. Padres de la cultura BIG BEAT

podcast.title: Abandonment of Traditional Instrumentation
podcast.body: For some German musicians, the path to creating a new and distinctive sound involved entirely abandoning the traditional instrumentation of rock and roll. Instead, they embraced the modern electronic music of their Fatherland as a means to establish a unique national musical identity. "To some, the only solution was to abandon the traditional instrumentation of Rock and Roll entirely. They had to embrace the modern electronic music of the Fatherland."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 6

podcast.title: Boiler Room Foundation
podcast.body: Electronic music found its equivalent to Tiny Desk in Boiler Room, which was founded in March 2010 by Blaise Bellville, a young British electronic music enthusiast. The platform was created to host DJ sessions for friends and broadcast them online, changing electronic music. "Y la música electrónica podríamos decir que tiene eso que valente."

srcs.episode: De Tiny Desk a Boiler Room: El Boom de los Conciertos en YouTube

podcast.title: Bowie's Berlin Period Fascination
podcast.body: By 1977, David Bowie had grown fascinated with electronic music, alongside German krautrock bands like Can, Neu!, and Kraftwerk. This fascination led him to West Berlin, where his "Berlin period" albums with Brian Eno and Tony Visconti adopted these new sounds as he sought to push musical boundaries. "He had also grown fascinated with electronic music and German crowd rock, bands like Cannes, Noy, and of course, Croftvirk."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Starman to Blackstar Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Bowie's Vision for the Future
podcast.body: David Bowie became deeply interested in the electronic methods of producing music, seeing them as the future, which motivated his move to Germany to further explore this muse. "He began to think that these electronic methods of producing music were the future."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Why Bowie Still Matters - Part 2

podcast.title: British Dominance in Post-Punk Era
podcast.body: By the early 1980s, Britain was saturated with electronic music, with bands like The Human League, Gary Numan, OMD, Ultravox, Visage, and Soft Cell leading the charge in the post-punk era. "Britain was a wash, electronic music in the post-punk era. There was, like I said, the human league and Gary Newman and OMD, plus bands like Ultravox and Visage and Soft Cell."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 7

podcast.title: Calculated and Minimalist Logos
podcast.body: Electronic music logos are characterized by a cold, squared, and mathematical aesthetic, resulting in designs that are more calculated and minimalist, exemplified by artists like AFX Twin and Justice. "Su carácter frío, cuadriculado y matemático nos deja logos más calculados y minimalistas."

srcs.episode: Cómo los Logos Definieron la Música ｜ Símbolos de Resistencia

podcast.title: Can's Influence on Producers
podcast.body: Can's unique fusion of rock with electronic elements exerted a significant influence on electronic music producers, demonstrating the band's impact beyond traditional rock genres and foreshadowing future developments in electronic sound. "han fluido también a la música electrónica y a productores de hip hop."

srcs.episode: CAN ｜ La Banda que (posiblemente) Inspiró a tu banda preferida

podcast.title: Cold, Paranoid Appeal (late 1970s/early 1980s)
podcast.body: Amidst the raw intensity of punk rock, a severe economic recession in the late 1970s and early 1980s, and the escalating Cold War, the concept of "cold, paranoid, hollow, dehumanized music" became particularly appealing to some audiences and artists. This aesthetic was strongly associated with the emerging electronic sound. "Under the all too real intensity of punk rock, the brutal recession of the late 70s and early 80s and the escalating cold war between America and the USSR, the idea of cold, paranoid, hollow, dehumanized music was actually pretty appealing for some people."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Commercial Electronic Focus in Utopian Virtual

podcast.body: During the grunge era, when rock-based remixes saw a decline, electronic outfits, along with industrial groups and some others, continued to utilize remixing. "Oh, it was still done for industrial groups, electronic outfits and a few others."

podcast.body: Damon Albarn's growing interest in electronic music led him to increasingly steer Blur's album Think Tank towards an electronic sound. podcast.title: Dazpán's Revolution in Electronic Music
podcast.body: Dazpán is credited with fundamentally changing the history of electronic music with their initial albums, particularly "homburmo." podcast.title: Definition of Electronic Music
podcast.body: Electronic music is defined as any music created using electronic instruments. This distinguishes it from acoustic music, which generates sound through physical elements like vibrating strings (guitar), air columns (flute), or percussive vibrations (drums). Electronic instruments, in contrast, generate music through electronic circuits or electricity. "la música electrónica es toda aquella que está hecha con instrumentos electrónicos."

podcast.title: Discovery by Generation X
podcast.body: Generation X discovered electronic music, which had existed outside the mainstream for years. "JNX discovered different flavors of Goth, an industrial, and electronic music."

podcast.title: Doctor Who Soundtrack as Foundation
podcast.body: The soundtrack for the 1960s "Doctor Who" series is recognized as one of the most important albums in electronic music history. It is credited with having laid the foundations for the electronic genre, preceding many works considered classical electronic music. "la bandas sonora del doctor H, de la serie de los años 60, es uno de los álbumes más importantes de la historia de la electrónica, uno de los álbumes que asentó las bases de la electrónica."

podcast.title: Dominance in Late 1990s
podcast.body: Electronic music, along with pop and hip-hop, dominated the music scene at the end of the 1990s, contributing to rock's perceived decline. "Pop, electronic eye and hip-hop had taken over. Rock itself had fallen into the doldrums."

podcast.title: Dominance in the 1980s (1980s)
podcast.body: The 1980s became synonymous with electronic music, largely due to the rising popularity and creative power of synthesizers. Musicians discovered that these new keyboards unleashed "new levels of creativity," shaping the decade's sound. "The 80s were all about electronic music. Musicians discovered the power of these new keyboards, which unleashed new levels of creativity."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Music vs Technology Over The Years

podcast.title: Early 1980s Experimentation
podcast.body: By the early 1980s, significant experimentation with electricity and new machines like computers and samplers led to an abundance of new and interesting music. This era saw music being created by machines, orchestrated by computers, and programmed by individuals with a punk ethos. "And by the time the decade ended, there was plenty of new and interesting music to go around."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 10

podcast.title: Early 2000s Oversaturation
podcast.body: The complexity and baroque style of electronic music reached an "absolutely unsustainable" point in the early 2000s, as exemplified by albums utilizing thousands of distinct sounds.

podcast.title: Early Development in West Germany
podcast.body: The first place where new electronic music truly took hold was in West Germany, fostering an avant-garde scene near Cologne by 1953, where experimentation with oscillators, wave generators, and tape loops flourished. "The place where this new electronic music really first caught on was in West Germany."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Forms and Exotic Sounds
podcast.body: Prior to the emergence of fully-fledged electronic music as a genre, there were early electronic instruments like the Theremin. These instruments were primarily used to generate "exotic sounds" or special effects rather than full musical compositions. It wasn't until later pioneers that the potential of electricity for creating entire musical pieces was fully realized. "era como una manera de generar sonidos exóticos, más allá de generar música."

podcast.title: Early Origins and Technological Advancement
podcast.body: Modern electronic music has a complex origin story that dates back to the 1940s, preceding the time when the necessary technology became affordable enough for young musicians to experiment with in the 1970s. "The birth of modern electronic music? Well, that has a rich and complicated origin story that stretches back to the 40s before the technology was cheap enough for young musicians to give it a go in the 70s."

podcast.title: Early Room-Sized Synthesizer (Unspecified)
podcast.body: Columbia University in New York possessed an early synthesizer that was so large it occupied an entire room, highlighting the massive scale of initial electronic music technology. "Columbia University in New York also had a synthesizer that filled an entire room."

podcast.title: Evolution in Björk's Sound
podcast.body: Björk's career is marked by a dynamic evolution within electronic music, transitioning from the raw energy of trip hop and harder electronic sounds in the mid-90s, influenced by collaborations with Nellee Hooper, to more experimental and industrial textures in *Homogenic*, before embracing organic, natural sounds in *Vespertine* and global influences in *Volta*. "ayuda a introducirse a Bjork a lo que serían las bases rítmicas del trip Hop y de la electrónica."

srcs.episode: Entender a Björk en 10 pasos

podcast.title: Evolution in the 80s
podcast.body: In the early 80s, electronic music saw the birth of techno in Detroit and house music from disco producers. These styles served as a "shock therapy" against the elaborate disco music of the late 70s, introducing simpler, repetitive sounds.

podcast.title: Evolution in the 90s
podcast.body: During the 1990s, electronic music increasingly intertwined with alternative and rock music. This was largely facilitated by the consolidation of modern, computerized recording systems that streamlined production processes, allowing independent and alternative groups to experiment with electronic sounds.

srcs.episode: Daft Punk: Como el Homework revolucionó la electrónica

podcast.title: Explosion in Popularity (late 90s)
podcast.body: Towards the end of the 1990s, electronic music and hip-hop continued to "explode in popularity," drawing interest away from rock music and influencing an increase in sales of keyboards, samplers, turntables, and mixers. "Meanwhile, hip hop and electronic had continued to explode in popularity."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 9: The Festivals

podcast.title: Extensive Use of Amen Break
podcast.body: Electronic music and its subgenre EDM have extensively employed the "Amen Break" sample, which is integrated into a vast number of tracks. This highlights the break's widespread influence across different forms of electronic music production. "It's all over hip-hop. It's all over electronic and EDM."

podcast.title: Extreme European Ramification
podcast.body: In Europe, the influx of American House and Techno music, combined with existing European electronic traditions and a tendency for extremization, led to the rapid proliferation of dozens of highly extreme and aggressive electronic styles. This included genres like Acid House, Trance, and Hardcore Techno, which created a profound disconnect between the "beast-like" European rave culture and the more tranquil electronic music found elsewhere. "aquí en Europa comenzó una ramificación en decenas, pero decenas y decenas de estilos electrónicos muy extremos y muy agresivos, reinterpretando todo eso."

podcast.title: First Portable Synth Transport (Unspecified)
podcast.body: The earliest portable synthesizer was so cumbersome and large that it required transport by rail car, illustrating the significant logistical challenges of early electronic instruments. "And the first portable synth had to be transported from place to place and I'm not getting about this on a rail car."

podcast.title: Founded by Ambient Music
podcast.body: Ambient music, as invented by Brian Eno, is noted for creating the foundational elements for many distinct genres of electronic music. "his invention of ambient music, which created the foundations for so many different genres of electronic music?"

podcast.title: French Electronic Scene in the 1990s
podcast.body: In the mid-1990s, the electronic music scene in France was largely characterized by a "discotecquero" (club-oriented or dance-oriented) style. This dominant trend meant that artists like Air, who pursued a more ambient and symphonic electronic sound, found it challenging to achieve commercial success within their home country, experiencing greater acclaim in the United Kingdom instead. "la electrónica francés era un poco tiraba por otros caminos. Era mucho mas discotefiero."

podcast.title: Gateway for Rock Fans
podcast.body: The inclusion of Big Beat tracks in movie and video game soundtracks, often mixed with metal groups, served as an entry point for many rock enthusiasts to discover and appreciate electronic music. "cosa que hizo que fue la puerta de entrada a la música electrónica de muchas aficionados al rock."

srcs.episode: Por qué el cine de los 2000 sonaba así? Big Beat

podcast.title: Genre Bridging
podcast.body: The Chemical Brothers are renowned for pushing beyond traditional electronic music, forging a path that expertly blends electronic sounds with rock music, particularly within the British indie scene. "van mucho más allá de la electrónica y han trabajado con gente importantísima y han hecho algo que se escapa ya de la electrónica para hacer casi un camino entre la electrónica y la música rock."

srcs.episode: Las mejores colaboraciones y remezclas de The Chemical Brothers

podcast.title: Giorgio Moroder's Inspirational Impact
podcast.body: Giorgio Moroder's experimental work with new synthesizers and his production of Donna Summer's "I Feel Love" in 1977 were extremely inspirational for those interested in electronic music. His robotic and futuristic sound served as a direct lineage to technopop bands like Depeche Mode, OMD, and the Human League, and provided a gateway to artists like Kraftwerk. "It became musicians looking for something new and different flock to it. It became a landmark in the development of electronic music for the masses."

podcast.title: Historical Roots (Theremin)
podcast.body: The origins of electronically generated music trace back to the Russian Revolution, when Bolshevik scientist Leon Theremin introduced a device that produced sounds using electric currents and magnetic fields. "The roots of electronically generated music goes far back as the Russian Revolution, when a full-shevik scientist named Leo Thereman introduced a device that used electric currents and magnetic fields to generate sounds."

podcast.title: Historical Samples
podcast.body: The album *Endtroducing.....* by DJ Shadow contains samples that have become integral to the history of both hip hop and electronic music. These specific sounds, carefully curated and repurposed, are now recognized as foundational elements within the historical narrative of electronic music. "O, de la historia de la electrónica. El resultado final, DJ's a Do hizo para la época una obra maestra."

podcast.title: Impact of Doctor Who Theme
podcast.body: The 1963 "Doctor Who Theme," a 100% electronic piece, was a musical revolution. It demonstrated that complete musical compositions could be made entirely with electronic means, inspiring many artists to pursue electronic music. This pivotal moment occurred years before the emergence of groups like Tangerine Dream, Kraftwerk, or the work of Jean-Michel Jarre. "la banda zona del doctor Jo y la canción del doctor Jo fue una revolución musical."

podcast.title: Impact of TONTO Synthesizer
podcast.body: The TONTO synthesizer, built by Malcolm Cecil and Robert Margouleff, had a massive influence on the world of electronic music by allowing for sounds and multi-track possibilities never before heard. Its capabilities led synthesizer manufacturers to significantly advance technology in the 1970s, producing smaller, faster, and cheaper electronic keyboards that in turn fueled the rise of Techno Pop. "Tonto influenced the shape of rock music and the use of the recording studio. And Tonto was a big reason synthesizing manufacturers worked so hard to advance the technology in the 1970s, creating these smaller, faster, cheaper electronic keyboards."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 1

podcast.title: Importance of Daphne Oram and Delia Derbyshire
podcast.body: The work of Daphne Oram and Delia Derbyshire at the BBC Radiophonic Workshop and in their independent careers is considered very important in the history of electronic music. They pioneered the use of early electronic equipment like sine wave oscillators, magnetic tape recorders, and tape manipulation to compose with synthetic sounds for radio, TV, and plays, shaping the foundations of the genre. "This is very important stuff in the history of electronic music, and she continued with her experimental compositions until 1975."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Hidden Figures

podcast.title: Influence of Brian Eno's School
podcast.body: The 1990s saw the "etapa de Brian Nino" (Brian Eno's stage/era) begin to heavily influence a "school" of electronic music that diverged from the discotheque sound. This period marked a growing appreciation for ambient and more symphonic forms of electronic music, particularly evident in German electronic music of the era, as exemplified by artists like Peter Culman. "un poco cuando la etapa de Brian Nino ya empezaba a generar mucha escuela en la electrónica que no era discotequera."

podcast.body: The Holidays' music has a distinct electronic component, incorporating synthesizers and drawing comparisons to groups known for their retro electronic sound. "grupos de poco entre electrónicos y desintitizadores."

podcast.body: Electronic elements are noted for their presence in Long Distance Calling's industrial rock, Jon Lein Stranger's lofi rap, and Franz Ferdinand's music after collaboration with a Cassius producer. "la parte más industrial del rock mezcla con la electrónica."

podcast.body: The intellectual electronic genre attracts a dedicated following, as exemplified by the rapid sell-out of Mark Peters' debut cassette album, "Innerland," within five minutes. podcast.body: This genre is noted for its intellectual and experimental subgenres, as exemplified by artists like Arca and influences in jazz. "electrónica más intelectual y más experimental."

podcast.title: John Frusciante's Work During Hiatus
podcast.body: During his time away from the Red Hot Chili Peppers, John Frusciante was actively involved in making electronic music, though he continued to practice guitar. This period marked a different creative direction for him before his return to rock music. "Practicing guitar is something I was always doing even though I'm making electronic music."

podcast.body: Faithless, the British band fronted by Maxi Jazz, is characterized as an electronic/hip-hop/dance band, highlighting electronic music as a core component of their sound. "Faithless, the British electronic slash hip-hop, slash dance, slash whatever band, tormented by a guy named Maxi Jazz."

podcast.body: The music in keygens was typically electronic and fast-paced, with accelerated tempos, similar to Rave or Trance music. This style was deliberately chosen to make users feel like "movie hackers," turning the bureaucratic task of entering an activation key into an adventurous cybernetic infiltration. "Esta música solía ser el electrónica y rápida, con tiempos acelerados musíilar a la música Rave o el Trance..."

podcast.title: Kraftwerk's Pioneering Role
podcast.body: Kraftwerk was incredibly important and influential in the overall idea of electronic music, with many subsequent developments, including Technopop, Industrial Music, and elements of Hip Hop, flowing from their work. They also advanced the idea that electronics were just as viable as guitars for making rock and roll. "Kraftwerk was incredibly important and incredibly influential when it came to the whole idea of electronic music."

podcast.title: Kraftwerk's Pioneering Role
podcast.body: The German Electronic Music band Kraftwerk pioneered sounds and techniques that influenced producers like Giorgio Moroder, who borrowed from them for his synthesizer-heavy productions in disco. "he borrowed a page from the German Electronic Music Band craft work."

podcast.title: Late 80s Decline
podcast.body: By the late 1980s, the electronic pop formula became "quite exhausted," leading to a significant decrease in quality material after 1987. Major electronic groups like Kraftwerk were also experiencing a downturn in their creative output, reflecting a general slump in electronic music production. "a final de los 80 esa forma la ya estaba bastante agotada ya prácticamente a partir del 87 ya tenemos muy poco material de calidad de electrónica pop tan famoso que se ha nacido en los 80."

podcast.title: Legacy of Machine-Made Acceptance
podcast.body: Despite its later reputation as "easy music," Big Beat played a crucial role in enabling a legion of rock fans and followers of other alternative genres to accept that music made with machines was not "a sin." "pero no olvidemos que esto sirvió para que una legión de seguidores del rock y otros generos más alternativos admitieran que la música hecha con máquinas no es ningún pecado."

podcast.title: Low Album's Influence on Synthesizer Music
podcast.body: David Bowie's "Low" album was a bold work that significantly spread the idea of synthesizer music beyond just what German artists were doing, influencing a new generation of post-punk musicians. podcast.body: Matt Bellamy incorporates forms of electronic music into his diverse playing style. "And as for style, he incorporates everything from prog rock to progressive metal to some forms of electronic, even even classical."

podcast.title: Mid-1990s Mainstream Rarity
podcast.body: In the mid-1990s, electronic music was still rarely heard on the radio and even less commonly seen on the charts, despite experiencing its most significant creative peak to date. "A mediados de la década de los 90, aún era raro escuchar música electrónica en la radio, y mucho más verlan las listas de éxitos."

podcast.title: Mid-20th Century Accessibility
podcast.body: It took until the mid-1960s for electronic music technology to advance sufficiently to become accessible to everyday musicians. "It wasn't until the mid-1960s that the technology had progressed to the point where it became accessible to everyday musicians."

podcast.title: Mid-90s Complexity
podcast.body: By the mid-90s, electronic music had evolved from the minimalist techno and house of the 80s into a more baroque, complicated, rapid, and elaborate form, incorporating numerous styles that sometimes seemed unrelated, including jazz and black music influences.

podcast.title: Origins in Nightclubs (1980s-1990s)
podcast.body: During the 1980s and 1990s, the vast majority of new electronic music genres, including Big Beat, originated from nightclubs, in contrast to later trends where new genres often emerge from the internet. "Aunque hoy en día, los nuevos generos de música electrónica suelen surgir de internet durante la década de los 80 a 90, la gran mayoría de ellos surgía de los club nocturnos."

podcast.title: Pioneering Composers and Equipment
podcast.body: The foundational work of Daphne Oram and Delia Derbyshire in the BBC Radiofonc Workshop, utilizing sine wave oscillators and magnetic tape machines before the advent of synthesizers, was crucial for the development of electronic music and EDM. Their experiments in composing with synthetic sounds paved the way for future innovations in the genre. "If you're into electronic music and EDM, you should know that these next two women are essential to what you'd listen to."

podcast.title: Post-War German Scene
podcast.body: In post-World War II Germany, following a period of denazification, young German musicians explored modernism and the avant-garde. By the 1950s, this evolution led to the creation of an experimental electronic music scene, primarily centered around universities and institutes that possessed the means to afford the then-exotic and expensive equipment. "By the 1950s, this had resulted in the creation of an experimental electronic music scene centered around the universities and institutes that could afford such exotic and expensive gear."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Predominantly European Style
podcast.body: Electronic music is a predominantly European style, with 90% of it before 1980 originating from Europe, establishing Europe as its "great capital." "En la música electrónica es un estilo mayoritario y predominantemente europeo."

podcast.title: Price Drop and Increased Power in 1970s
podcast.body: Throughout the 1970s, the sophistication and power of electronic instruments dramatically increased, while their prices simultaneously began to decrease, making them affordable for beginner musicians by the late 1970s. "In the 1970s, the sophistication and power of these instruments increased dramatically at the same time prices started to come down. By the late 70s, even the beginner musician could afford one."

srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 7

podcast.title: Progressive Electronic Influence in Dreampunk
podcast.body: Dreampunk draws significant influences from progressive electronic music, contributing to its dreamlike and abstract soundscapes. "influencias de la música ambiental y la electrónica progresiva."

podcast.title: Reinvention by Trip Hop
podcast.body: The arrival of Massive Attack's *Blue Lines* in 1991, with its complex fusion of electronic elements with pop, reggae, and jazz, marked the "starting shot" for the reinvention of modern electronic music, which previously seemed an "unthinkable" blend to critics in the 80s. "el pisto letazo de salida de la reinvención de la música la itónica moderna."

podcast.title: Resurgence of Electronic Bases in Music (Mid-2000s)
podcast.body: The mid-2000s saw a resurgence of electronic bases in music, which were mixed with pop, rock, and other styles. This trend provided a context for bands like Mios to update their sound by incorporating electronic elements. "A mitad del 2000 ya hubo un resurgir de todas esas bases electrónicas mezcladas con pop y con un rock y con otros estilos."

podcast.title: Robot/Machine Creation
podcast.body: The radical idea of delegating the creation of music to robots and machines was perceived as the ultimate "punk" act. This innovative approach significantly contributed to the development and distinct character of the electronic music sound. "And what could be more punk, more radical than turning the creation of music over to robots and machines?"

podcast.title: Roskilde Representation
podcast.body: Electronic music is one of the genres represented at the Roskilde festival, which hosts approximately 180 different acts for up to 130,000 people. "There's rock, there's folk, there's electronic and hip hop. They're all represented in one way or the other."

podcast.title: Shift from Guitars to Keyboards (1980s)
podcast.body: As the 1980s dawned, a widespread desire emerged to "ditch their guitars and get into the 21st century a little bit early by buying cheapos synthesizers and making the music of the future." Keyboards and other electronic instruments consequently became the primary focus of this new musical direction, although some artists still advocated for the guitar's continued relevance. "As the 1980s beckoned, it seemed that everybody wanted to ditch their guitars and get into the 21st century a little bit early by buying cheapos synthesizers and making the music of the future."

podcast.title: Subgenre Diversity on Boiler Room
podcast.body: Boiler Room quickly adapted to program sessions across various genres dominating the British dance scene, including Garage, Techno, and Dub. Today, almost any electronic subgenre finds a platform on Boiler Room. "Semana la trasemana fueron programando sesiones de los generos que dominaban la escena de baile al de Groove Británica, Garage, Techno, Dab, Feroz Formato, pronto traspasó las fronteras británicas."

podcast.title: Subgenre Emergence and Underground Nature
podcast.body: During its creative peak in the mid-1990s, electronic music saw the emergence of numerous subgenres like drum and bass and goa trance. These styles, though influential, typically remained confined to nightclubs, given their experimental and raw nature, and were primarily aimed at urban subcultures and raves rather than a mass audience. "Y eso que estaba viviendo su mayor pico de creatividad hasta el momento, y no paraban de emergir sub-generos como el drama bass, el yucagara echualtrance."

podcast.title: Surge in Interest in West Germany (Post-Mini Moog)
podcast.body: Following the 1971 invention of the Mini Moog, there was a huge surge in interest in electronic music within West Germany, making it a hotbed for experimentation and the emergence of leading electronic groups like Kraftwerk. "Again, people went nuts in West Germany. There was a huge surge in interest in electronic music."

srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 3: Industrial

podcast.title: Symbiotic Creative Contribution
podcast.body: A major source of creativity in contemporary music stems from the subtle and smooth symbiosis between alternative music and electronic music. This fusion is bringing a significant creative input to much of today's music, as evidenced by artists like Nicolas Jaar, James Blake, Bon Iver, and Moderat. "esta nueva symbiosis entre la música alternativa y la música electrónica, de una manera muy sutila y muy suave, es lo que nos están dando un gran aporte creativo y en día gran parte de la música."
